daivata-liṅga
(‘liṅga [of gods]’)
------------------------------------------
Śiva, the third deity of the Hindu Trinity, is always worshipped as a लिङ्ग, a cylindrical symbol with a spherical top. The word ‘liṅga’ means that Supreme Power into which the whole universe dissolves at the end of च्रेअतिओन् (‘līyate asmin iti liṅgaḥ’).
A लिङ्ग can be cala (movable) or acala (immovable). The liṅgas in शिव temples are always acala. Such acala-liṅgas can be of several varieties—4 or 6 or even 9—of which the दैवत-लिङ्ग (also called ‘daivika-लिङ्ग’) is one. Since it is supposed to have been established by the gods of हेअवेन् it gets this name (daiva = related to gods).
Its shape resembles that of a flame of light and suggests to our मिन्द् hands folded in supplication. Its surface is rugged and contains marks of टङ्क (hammer) and śūla (spear). There is no ब्रह्मसूत्र mark.
See also BRAHMASŪTRA and LIṄGA.

daiva
(‘related to deva,’ ‘luck or fate’)
------------------------------------------
Throughout the history of mankind, some kind of belief in destiny, in the unseen hand of fate, seems to have existed. The Hindus have been no exception to this phenomenon.
The word ‘daiva’ has been derived from ‘deva’, a god or a superior being or a supernatural power. In effect, it means the unseen power of fate (adṛṣṭa).
The धर्मशास्त्रस् and the पुराणस् have discussed in detail, the question whether दैव is more powerful or puruṣakāra (human effort). Three different views have emerged:
Daiva is all-powerful;
Human effort is superior;
Both have an equal place in our life.
Since दैव (fate or luck) is generally interpreted as the cumulative effect of our past karmas tending to give a particular direction in this life, the third view seems to be more reasonable.
See also ADṚṢṬA.

daivīsampat
(‘divine wealth’)
------------------------------------------
The Bhagavadgītā is a cardinal scripture of हिन्दुइस्म् revered by all sections of the Hindus. It has also attracted the attention of many a spiritual seeker and savant from the great religions of the world.
The sixteenth chapter of this work deals with two archetypes among the human beings—the āsuric or the demoniac and the daivī or the divine beings. The former are hostile to all moral and spiritual values whereas the latter are fully receptive to them.
These moral and spiritual values listed in this chapter (1

) are called ‘daivīsampad’ or ‘daivīsampat’, a wealth (sampat = wealth) that ultimately leads to the attainment of the divine state (daivī = divine).
They are: abhaya (fearlessness), sattvasaṁśuddhi (purity of the heart), ज्ञान-योग-vyavasthiti (steadfastness in knowledge and devotion), दान (benevolence), दम (control of senses), यज्ञ (worship), स्वाध्याय (study of the scriptures), तपस् (austerity of body, speech and मिन्द्), ārjava (uprightness), अहिṁसा (non-violence), सत्य (truth), akrodha (freedom from anger), त्याग (renunciation), śānti (tranquillity), apaiśuna (aversion to slander), bhūteṣu दया (compassion towards all living beings), aloluptva (freedom from sensuality), mārdava (gentleness), hrī (modesty), acāpala (steadiness), तेजस् (vigour), kṣamā (forgiveness), dhṛti (fortitude), शौच (purity), adroha (harmlessness), nātimānitā (freedom from vanity).
It is obvious that these great qualities when practised properly and imbibed, will raise all human beings from the brute level to divine heights.
See also BHAGAVADGĪTĀ.

daiva-vivāha
(‘marriage [related to the rite] of gods’)
------------------------------------------
Vivāha or मर्रिअगे has been a very ancient institution right from the times of the Ṛgveda. The mantras used in the मर्रिअगे ceremonies of the dvijas (‘the twice-born,’ the ब्राह्मणस्, the kṣattriyas and the vaiśyas) even in the modern days draw heavily from the Vedic and allied literature.
Of the eight forms of मर्रिअगे depicted in the ancient works like the गृह्यसूत्रस्, the दैव-विवाह is also one and is classed among the superior varieties. It is described as gifting one’s daughter, after properly decorating her, to a priest who has officiated in the sacrifice. It was almost like दक्षिणा or sacrificial fee.
It was called ‘daiva’ since the sacrifice was for appeasing the देवस् or gods like इन्द्र and the gifting of the girl took place as a part of the sacrifice.
This form of मर्रिअगे seems to have been discouraged and hence disappeared in course of time.
See also VIVĀHA.
